analysis.one_liner: Permanently limits the FCC's power to regulate broadband providers like phone companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to a House subcommittee in January 2015 and sat there until the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law that broadband internet is a lightly regulated 'information service,' not a 'common carrier' like the telephone system. That would permanently block the FCC from using its phone-era Title II authority over broadband — the legal basis for rules requiring internet providers to treat all web traffic equally. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee's communications subcommittee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Broadband providers — cable and telephone companies such as Comcast, Verizon, and AT&T — would gain a permanent statutory shield from common-carrier duties, including net neutrality rules against blocking, slowing, or charging websites for faster delivery. The bill's findings argue this preserves tens of billions of dollars of broadband investment that providers claim Title II would discourage [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Adds broadband internet access service to the legal definition of an 'information service,' the lighter-touch category the FCC had historically used, and states that a provider of an information service may not be treated as a telecommunications carrier or required to offer its service as a telecommunications service [S2] [S3].

Excludes providers of information services and advanced telecommunications capability from the definitions of 'common carrier,' 'telecommunications carrier,' and 'telecommunications service,' closing off the FCC's Title II common-carrier authority over them [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings section argues that prior FCC information-service rulings in 1998, 2002, 2005, and 2007 — upheld by the Supreme Court in the 2005 Brand X case — unleashed tens of billions of dollars in broadband investment that common-carrier regulation would not have [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Internet users would bear the cost: the bill would strip the FCC's strongest legal tool for enforcing net neutrality, leaving the FCC with only weak 'ancillary jurisdiction' over broadband. Without common-carrier rules, providers could lawfully block, slow, or charge websites and services for faster access, costs that would flow to consumers and online businesses.

drawbacks.text: By excluding broadband from every common-carrier definition, the bill would prevent the FCC from imposing the open-internet protections — no blocking, no throttling, no paid prioritization — that it later applied when it reclassified broadband under Title II in 2015 [S2].

The bill's own economic case rests on the industry's claim that Title II would 'severely harm broadband investment'; supporters of Title II disputed that, pointing out that providers invested heavily in the decades when the FCC had stronger authority over them — an assertion of harm the bill states but does not prove [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to providers — legal certainty and freedom from utility-style rules — is real and concentrated. The cost is diffuse: the public's ability to enforce equal treatment of internet traffic would rest on a much weaker legal foundation. The bill presents its investment argument in its findings, but an honest reading is that it resolves a contested regulatory question permanently and in the providers' favor, before any committee or floor debate weighed the evidence.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications and Technology Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Latta introduced the bill on January 12, 2015, joined as an original cosponsor by Reps. Walter Jones, Randy Weber of Texas, and Charles Rangel, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
Four days later it was referred to the subcommittee on Communications and Technology, which was its last action; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed [S5].
The bill had only three cosponsors and never advanced out of subcommittee, so no committee or floor vote ever recorded where members stood [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband users and net-neutrality supporters are better off that the bill died: the FCC's 2015 order reclassifying broadband under Title II — which the bill was written to overrule by statute — was adopted in February 2015 and stood, keeping common-carrier open-internet rules in place. The providers the bill was written to shield never got their statutory protection.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it in its findings as protecting broadband investment from Title II regulation.

for.name: Reps. Walter Jones, Randy Weber, and Charles Rangel
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: Broadband providers (cable and telephone companies)
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against Title II reclassification and for legislation locking in the light-touch information-service classification; the bill tracks that position clause by clause.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; chair never scheduled a markup
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Communications and Technology Subcommittee and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both Republican cosponsors were joined by one Democrat, Rep. Charles Rangel; no vote ever occurred, so no fuller party breakdown exists [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have written the industry's preferred light-touch classification into statute, permanently barring the FCC from applying common-carrier duties such as no-blocking, no-throttling, and paid-prioritization rules. Its interest runs against the public's on this bill because it seeks to remove the strongest legal check on how it treats its own customers' traffic [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Internet edge companies (streaming, search, e-commerce, startups)
industries.note: These companies depend on the ability to reach consumers without paying for priority; by closing off Title II authority, the bill would have left them exposed to access fees or discrimination by broadband providers, costs ultimately passed to users. Their interest runs with the public's [S2].
